title: "He abused me" (3–6)
hookLine: hatred never ceases by hatred, only by not-hatred; this is an old rule (Dhammapada 5)
last: MANOPUBBANGAMA — THE WHEEL FOLLOWS THE OX.

cards: Two in the morning. Someone lies awake, replaying it. What was said at the meeting.
The look on a face. The perfect answer that came too late. The scene has been turned over so often it's worn smooth, like a stone in a pocket, and it still stings each time.
The Dhammapada's third verse puts that replay into a single line, as if it had been listening at the bedroom door.

teach.b: Verse three, in Müller's English: “‘He abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me,’—in those who harbour such thoughts hatred will never cease.”
Verse four is its twin: in those who don't harbor such thoughts, hatred will cease. Notice where the problem is placed. Not only in what the other person did, but in the replay.
The verse doesn't say the insult didn't happen.
It says hatred lives on in the harboring.

teach.h: VERSE FIVE: BY NOT HATING BACK.
teach.b: Then verse five: “hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love.” Müller wrote love. The Pali word is averena: by non-hatred, by not hating back.
It's quieter than love, and maybe more realistic: you don't have to feel warm toward the person, you just stop feeding the fire.
The verse ends: this is an old rule. In the Pali, an eternal law: not something new, but an ancient rule.
The commentary sets verse five in a story of two women whose rivalry ran on through lifetime after lifetime, each taking revenge for the last, until the Buddha stopped the cycle.
Verse six belongs to a well-known quarrel among the monks of Kosambi, who split over a small matter of rules.
It says, roughly, that people forget everyone comes to an end here, and those who remember it let their quarrels settle.
So chapter one gives two tools for the 2am replay: notice that the hatred lives in the harboring, and remember how short all of this is.

how: Verse five of the Dhammapada is often recited; teachers use verses three to six to show that resentment is kept alive by rehearsing it, and ended by not answering hatred with hatred.

o: by not hating back, without having to force love
by paying back a wrong with a fair punishment
by waiting until the other person says sorry

games.q: match the pieces of verses three to six.
p: the replay: he abused me, he robbed me
by non-hatred, by not hating back

s: the Pali of verse five says hatred ceases by love
Müller wrote love; the Pali averena means by non-hatred, by not hating back.
verse five calls this an old rule, or an eternal law
the Pali calls it sanantano: ancient, or eternal.
verse three says the insult never really happened
it says hatred lives on in those who harbor the thought.

games.q: you're the Buddha. the monks of Kosambi are quarreling and, when you try to make peace, they tell you to stay out of it. what do you do?
o: leave them and go off alone to the forest.
take one side and settle it.
games.why: in the Vinaya's telling, he left and spent time alone in the forest. the lay people then stopped supporting the quarreling monks until they made peace.

practice: Let a small old grudge come to mind, not the biggest, a mild one, and hear its sentence once, your own version of “he abused me, he robbed me.”
Instead of replaying it, feel what it does in the jaw, the shoulders, the stomach, and breathe into that place.
You don't have to forgive anyone right now; just try not feeding it for the length of this sit, and when the replay starts again, come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: Averena. By non-hatred: the old rule, in verses three to six, that only not-hatred ends the thought “he abused me” that keeps hatred alive.

orig.note: Pali: by non-hatred, from verse five: hatred is calmed by non-hatred.

carryVoice: Your line: hatred ends by not-hatred. The stone in the pocket can rest. That's day one hundred fifty-nine.

sources.q: 'He abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me,'--in those who harbour such thoughts hatred will never cease.
